# Really Hard to Find A/C Leak on 2007 Mustang

Diagnosing a slow refrigerant leak in a 2007 Mustang V6 is often less about finding a massive hole and more about spotting subtle pressure differentials that betray the system's integrity. You have a vehicle where the charge holds for only five days, indicating a significant loss despite what appears to be a tight seal under static conditions. The fact that your electronic leak detector consistently points only to the Schrader valves is a classic false positive scenario, yet it provides a critical clue about where your diagnostic efforts should focus next.

The high side of your A/C system leaking significantly more than the low side suggests a specific pressure-driven issue. In many automotive HVAC systems, the Schrader valve on the high side is subject to much higher pressures than the low side. If these valves are indeed leaking, it is often because the internal seals have degraded or the brass body has been compromised by vibration over 17 years of service. The difficulty you faced removing themâfinding them "frozen" tightâis not uncommon. These fittings can seize due to corrosion or simply overtightening during previous maintenance. Before you assume they are irreparable, try penetrating oil and a proper breaker bar; forcing them out with excessive torque often damages the flare seating surface, making reassembly impossible without specialized tools.

Your vacuum test results are telling, but they require precise interpretation. You evacuated the system to near -30 inches of mercury and held it for 50 minutes (30 on the pump, 20 off) with no loss. Then, you removed the high side hose, waited 20 minutes, and observed zero vacuum loss. This specific sequence is crucial. By isolating the high-side service port while the low side remained connected to the rest of the circuit, you effectively tested the integrity of the compressor, condenser, receiver/drier (on the low side), and expansion valve/orifice tube assembly. The fact that the system held vacuum perfectly when the high side was open to atmosphere after the pump was turned off confirms that the compressor itself is not leaking internally, nor is there a major leak in the condenser or evaporator.

However, the moment you reconnected everything and lost pressure within five days, the data points back to the service ports or the lines immediately attached to them. If the Schrader valves are indeed the source, replacing them is the logical next step. You mentioned that the low-side valve is part of the receiver/drier assembly. This is a common design in Mustangs of this era; if that valve is leaking, the entire receiver/drier unit must be replaced. It is not just about swapping the Schrader stem; the internal desiccant bag often needs replacing to ensure moisture doesn't clog the expansion valve downstream.

For the high side, the valve is integrated into the condenser outlet hose assembly. Replacing this entire hose assembly is expensive but necessary if the valve body is cracked or the O-ring seals are blown. Attempting to weld a patch onto these aluminum lines usually fails due to thermal stress and vibration. The trade-off here is cost versus reliability: buying a new high-side hose assembly ensures a fresh seal, whereas trying to salvage the old one risks recurring leaks that will waste more money on refrigerant charges later.

Before committing to a full replacement of all components, consider a final diagnostic step often overlooked: oil dye. If you suspect microscopic leaks in the lines rather than just the valves, injecting UV dye and running the system for a day might reveal bubbles forming around the valve stems or line fittings that an electronic detector misses due to airflow masking the signal. Once identified, these are easy to patch with self-sealing epoxy or replace the specific fitting. If the vacuum holds but pressure drops immediately upon recharging, you have confirmed the leak is external to the main system components and likely resides at the service ports you've already identified.
